lesson_title: The Classroom and the Stadium: Density vs Distribution
hook_text: Forty learners in a classroom. Forty in a stadium. Same people, different everything.
clip_script: Put forty learners in a normal classroom. Now put the same forty in a soccer stadium. Same number of people, completely different feeling — and that feeling is DENSITY. People divided by space. Crowded in the classroom, lost in the stadium. Now the second experiment, the one people miss. Keep everyone in the stadium and arrange them two ways. First spread all forty evenly around the stands. Then bring all forty into one huddle in a single corner, leaving the rest empty. The density hasn't changed at all — forty people, same stadium. But the PATTERN has completely changed, and that pattern is DISTRIBUTION. So density is a number: how crowded. Distribution is a picture: where they are. And here's why it matters at home. South Africa's average density is about fifty people per square kilometre — a figure that describes precisely nowhere, because it's the empty Karoo and packed Soweto stirred into one number. Gauteng is under two per cent of the land and about a quarter of the people. The Northern Cape is nearly a third of the land and about two per cent of the people. Averages hide the whole story.
visual_style: Overhead shot of a packed classroom dissolving into a stadium: forty dots first scattered evenly, then sliding into one corner, with a density counter that never changes.
pacing: Two quick experiments, a beat on the unchanged counter, punchy national numbers at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to read South Africa's population map like a geographer.
